activities.caption: pin the resting potential on the millivolt scale
activities.name: nbPotentialPlace

config.prompt: An action potential reverses the axon's membrane potential to +30 mV for about a millisecond. Where does the membrane sit at rest (mV)?
config.why: About −70 mV — the resting potential is the sodium–potassium pump's accumulated work, and the spike is its brief reversal.
config.context: The pulse is all-or-nothing: a weak stimulus fires fewer spikes, not weaker ones — intensity is encoded in frequency.

activities.anchor: every drug that affects the mind acts here
activities.caption: pair each chemical with its synaptic move
activities.name: nbDrugMatch

config.prompt: The 20-nanometre gap is where mind meets molecule — pair each player with its move:

pairs.right: prolongs serotonin's stay in the gap
excites vs inhibits — the chemicals are polarity-specific

config.why: Synapses are one-way valves (vesicles only on the sending side), decision points (excitation must win), and amplifiers (thousands of transmitter molecules per vesicle).

activities.caption: file the eye's parts by whose job they are
activities.name: nbEyeBuckets

config.prompt: Receptors or optics? File each fact:

items.label: about 120 million, extremely sensitive, no colour
own dim, colourless night and peripheral vision
packed into the fovea where you read this text
the cornea — about two-thirds of the focusing
adjusts the pupil's diameter, trading depth of field against light

config.why: A sense is always transduction — one form of energy converted into spikes the brain can count; the ear's hair cells and the nose's olfactory receptors follow the same recipe.

activities.anchor: rods see colour and cones work at night
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the retina answer
activities.name: nbRodSpot

config.prompt: This photoreceptor answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Cones need brighter light but come in three wavelength types: red, green and blue.
Cones own colour and daytime detail at the fovea.
Rods are so sensitive that bright light saturates them.
Rods own colour vision at night; cones take over in the dark.
A faint star is easier to see slightly off-centre — its image lands on rods.
config.correction: It is the reverse: rods own DIM, COLOURLESS night and peripheral vision; cones own colour and daytime detail.
config.why: The anatomy explains it: cones need brighter light but carry the three colour types; rods saturate in brightness but excel in the dark.

activities.anchor: affect target cells carrying the matching receptor
activities.caption: true or false — the broadcast network
activities.name: nbHormoneJudge

statements.s: Hormones affect only target cells carrying the matching receptor; every other cell ignores them.
Nerves are fast, specific and short-lived; hormones are slower, widespread and lasting.
statements.why: Milliseconds versus seconds to days — every animal with both uses the pair exactly this way.

statements.s: Hormones reach their targets by travelling along nerves.
statements.why: They travel in the bloodstream, secreted by glands — pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenal, gonads.

statements.s: The pituitary is the master gland — the brain commands the other glands through it.
statements.why: And hormones feed back onto the brain: adrenaline is the felt ingredient of fear.

activities.anchor: The canonical control loop has three parts
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the control loop
activities.name: nbLoopCloze

config.text: The canonical control loop has three parts: %%0%% that detect a deviation, a %%1%% %%2%% that compares it to the set point, and %%3%% that correct it. Negative feedback %%4%%; positive feedback drives one-shot events — like childbirth — to completion.
config.hint: Each deviation automatically calls up its own correction — that is why the set point holds.

activities.anchor: where a reflex arc finishes in 20 milliseconds
activities.caption: two solutions, one physics problem — drag across kingdoms
activities.name: nbTropismCompare

config.prompt: Coordination, animal vs plant — drag the divider:

before.label: reflex arc
before.text: Detect, transmit, respond — finished in about 20 milliseconds. Animals flee.

after.label: tropism
after.text: The same three steps with growth instead of movement: auxin migrates to the shaded side, and a tropism takes hours.

config.why: Both systems detect a stimulus, transmit a signal, produce a response — two solutions to the same physics problem of staying alive in a directional world.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the brain's power draw
activities.name: nbWattsEstimate

config.prompt: The brain is 2% of body mass burning about 20% of the resting energy budget. Roughly how many watts does it run on?
config.why: About 20 watts — a dim light bulb — computing with an efficiency modern supercomputers running brain simulations cannot approach.
config.context: 86 billion neurons, around 100 trillion synapses — thinking is expensive, which is why brains evolved only where the payoff beat the bill.
